title: Kinetics of sliding-window quantum error correction
authors: Adithya Sriram, Charles Stahl, Aleksander Kubica, Yaodong Li
abstract: Practical implementations of quantum error correction (QEC) require rapid measurement and continuous processing of the syndrome information in order to prevent a backlog of unprocessed data. While ``static'' QEC is theoretically well understood via mappings to equilibrium statistical mechanics models, such an understanding of ``real-time'' QEC is currently lacking. Here, we study the kinetics of sliding window decoding (SWD), an implementation of real-time decoding that acts on temporally local windows of noisy syndrome information and commits to corrections irreversibly at a nonzero rate. We propose an effective description of SWD in terms of a stochastic kinetic process, where $\mathbb{Z}_2$-charged point particles undergo parity-conserving reaction and diffusion. This model describes dynamics at length and time scales large compared to the window size $W$, whereas physics at scales smaller than $W$ leads to nontrivial $W$-dependent scaling of the effective parameters. We identify the rate of decoding $1/W$ as a relevant perturbation to the decodable phase. We also show broad applicability of our results by changing many microscopic details of SWD without affecting the effective description.
summary: This paper develops an effective kinetic theory to describe how quantum error correction performs in real time using sliding windows. It models the syndrome information evolution as a parity-conserving reaction-diffusion process for $\mathbb{Z}_2$ charges. The key finding is that this system exhibits universal crossover scaling between different operational regimes, providing crucial insights into hardware limitations.
main_problem: The study addresses the kinetics of Quantum Error Correction (QEC) in a real-time setting, moving beyond static theoretical models.
main_result: Sliding-Window Decoding (SWD) can be effectively described by a stochastic kinetic process involving parity-conserving reaction and diffusion of $\mathbb{Z}_2$-charged point particles.
method: The authors derive an effective description by analyzing the dynamics over large length and time scales relative to the window size $W$, connecting microscopic SWD processes to macroscopic kinetic models.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using topological CSS codes (e.g., 1D repetition code, 2D toric code) undergoing syndrome measurement via a sliding temporal window ($W$). Errors manifest as $\mathbb{Z}_2$-charged point particles whose dynamics are tracked.
key_observables: Memory Time ($t_{	ext{mem}}$), logical failure probability ($P_{	ext{fail}}(t; W, L)$), and the density of domain walls ($ho_{DW}$).
important_parameters: Window size $W$, system length $L$, error rate $p$, and the decoding rate $1/W$. The crossover between regimes defined by $W$ vs. $L$ is crucial.
main_assumptions: The effective description holds for scales much larger than the window size $W$; the analysis often assumes quasi-local motion of defects; and specific decoders (like MWPM) are used as the basis for comparison.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SWD mechanism with temporal windows, worldlines of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ charges distinguishing fast/slow processes, and data collapse confirming universal crossover scaling laws between different physical regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for real-time QEC kinetics, models SWD as a reaction-diffusion process, derives scaling relations for memory time and diffusion constant across various length scales ($W$ vs $L$), and validates this effective theory using multiple code types (1D, 2D) and noise models.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful connection between non-equilibrium statistical mechanics (reaction-diffusion kinetics) and the practical performance limits of quantum computation hardware, offering quantitative predictions for error thresholds based on temporal processing constraints.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Illustration of the sliding-window decoder, for the first few rounds. The error and the correction together form closed loops in the bulk, with possible termination on the temporal boundary between the “buffer” and the “future” regions. Within each round, only correction operations in the “commit” region are turned into physical corrections; those in the “buffer” region serve as a look-ahead to improve decoding accuracy. (b) Worldlines of Z2 charges. Fast pair nucleation and annihilation events occur within O(W) time scale (gray), whereas slow processes persist over many decoding rounds (black), and contribute to decoding failure.
